back: Small amounts of soluble substances, such as the dyes in ink or food colourings, by how far the solvent carries them up the paper.

front: Three rules for setting up paper chromatography
back: Draw the base line in pencil; keep the solvent level below the base line; cover the beaker with a lid.

front: Why do substances travel different distances in chromatography?
back: They have different solubilities in the solvent (and different attractions to the paper): the more soluble a substance, the further it moves.
One spot: probably pure. Several spots: a mixture. Same height as a known substance in the same solvent: probably that substance.
$R_f = \dfrac{\text{distance moved by substance}}{\text{distance moved by solvent}}$, both measured from the base line.
Always between 0 and 1; no units; constant for a substance in a given solvent, so it can be compared with data.
A chemical sprayed on a dried chromatogram that reacts with colourless substances (such as amino acids) to form coloured, visible spots.

front: What are the **base line** and the **solvent front**?
back: Base line: the pencil line where the samples are spotted. Solvent front: the furthest point the solvent reaches.

front: **ZIMSEC.** How does thin-layer chromatography (TLC) differ from paper chromatography?
back: It uses a plate coated with a thin layer of silica gel instead of paper; it is faster and gives sharper, better-separated spots.
Identifying food colourings (and banned dyes); comparing inks in forensic work; checking the purity of medicines; identifying amino acids from proteins.
